content: A medical guideline, also referred to as a clinical guideline, clinical protocol, or clinical practice guideline, is a document designed to assist healthcare professionals in making decisions regarding the diagnosis, management, and treatment of specific medical conditions. These guidelines have been utilized throughout the history of medicine, spanning thousands of years. However, unlike traditional approaches that often relied on authority or custom, modern medical guidelines are grounded in evidence-based medicine, which involves a thorough evaluation of current scientific evidence. Modern clinical guidelines typically include summarized consensus statements and address practical issues in clinical practice. They aim to identify, summarize, and evaluate the best available evidence and the most up-to-date data on prevention, diagnosis, prognosis, therapy (including medication dosages), risk-benefit analysis, and cost-effectiveness. These guidelines also define key clinical questions and outline all potential decision options and their associated outcomes. Some guidelines incorporate decision-making or computational algorithms to streamline clinical processes, integrating these tools with the clinical judgment and expertise of healthcare providers. Many guidelines categorize treatment options into classes to assist clinicians in selecting the most appropriate course of action. The objectives of clinical guidelines include standardizing medical care, improving the quality of care, minimizing risks to patients, healthcare providers, insurers, and health plans, and achieving an optimal balance between cost and medical outcomes such as effectiveness, specificity, sensitivity, and resolution. The use of guidelines by healthcare providers, including hospitals, has been repeatedly shown to be an effective means of achieving these objectives, although they are not the sole method. To facilitate the implementation of medical guidelines, specialized software known as guideline execution engines has been developed. These tools work in conjunction with electronic medical record systems. The Guideline Interchange Format (GLIF) is a computer-based representation format for clinical guidelines that can be utilized with such engines. Despite their utility, some simple clinical practice guidelines are not consistently followed in practice. Studies have shown that providing nurses or other medical assistants with a checklist of recommended procedures can help ensure that attending physicians are reminded of overlooked procedures in a timely manner. The guideline-based approach to healthcare is relatively recent, originating in the United States during the 1990s. Guidelines are typically developed at national or international levels by medical associations or governmental organizations, such as the US Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality. Local healthcare providers may create their own guidelines or adapt them from existing high-level guidelines. In the United States, the National Guideline Clearinghouse maintains a catalog of high-quality guidelines published by various organizations, primarily professional physician associations. In the United Kingdom, clinical practice guidelines are primarily published by the National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE). In the Netherlands, specialist and primary care guidelines are published by the CBO and NHG, respectively. In Germany, the German Agency for Quality in Medicine (AEZQ) coordinates a national program for disease management guidelines. These organizations are members of the Guidelines International Network (G-I-N), a global non-profit association dedicated to clinical practice guidelines. G-I-N also manages the International Guideline Library, the largest web-based database of medical guidelines worldwide. Standards for the development and reporting of clinical practice guidelines are available. Part of the guideline creation process involves gathering and assessing all relevant research, often using frameworks such as the GRADE system. Techniques like decision analysis and nominal group techniques can enhance the validity of clinical practice guidelines. The methodologies used in guideline development continue to evolve. Guidelines are increasingly being structured in a computable format to adapt rapidly to emerging evidence, such as during the COVID-19 pandemic. However, guidelines may lose their clinical relevance over time as new research emerges. Studies indicate that up to 20% of strong recommendations, particularly those based on expert opinion rather than clinical trials, may eventually be retracted. Conflicting guidelines can be summarized and mapped in a structured manner to help identify and resolve discrepancies. The National Academy of Medicine (formerly the Institute of Medicine) has published recommendations for assessing the quality of guidelines. These recommendations emphasize transparency, management of conflicts of interest, appropriate composition of guideline development groups, systematic reviews, evidence quality, strength of recommendations, clear articulation of recommendations, external review, and regular updates. An alternative framework for guideline assessment is the AGREE II tool. In cases where guidelines present conflicting recommendations, physicians should strive to ensure that patients understand there may be more than one valid approach based on the current evidence. System-level changes, such as legislation to create safe harbors, have been proposed to address these challenges.
